No t e s
1. 
The Non-Delegation, Doctrine After the New Deal. Since the Schechter 
case the Supreme Court has not invalidated a single statute on the basis of 
excessive delegation. This result cannot be explained by a tightening of the 
criteria that Congress gives to agencies for when to exercise power.
In Yakus v. United States, 321 U.S. 414 (1944), the Court upheld 
Congress’s World War II delegation of authority to control prices, which was 
implemented by the Office of Price Administration (OPA). The Emergency 
Price Control Act directed the Administrator to fix prices in order “to stabilize 
commodity prices [and] prevent war-time inflation and its enumerated 
disruptive causes and effects. In addition the prices established must be fair 
and equitable, and in fixing them the Administrator is directed to give due 
consideration, so far as practicable, to prevailing prices during the designated 
base period, with prescribed administrative adjustments to compensate for 
enumerated disturbing factors affecting prices.”
The Court distinguished the Emergency Price Control Act from the 
National Industrial Recovery Act and explained: “Only if we could say that 
there is an absence of standards for the guidance of the Administrator’s action, 
so that it would be impossible in a proper proceeding to ascertain whether the 
will of Congress has been obeyed, would we be justified in overriding its choice 
of means for effecting its declared purpose of preventing inflation.” The Court 
upheld the Emergency Price Control Act because it prescribed standards 
“sufficiently definite and precise to enable Congress, the courts and the public 
to ascertain whether the Administrator, in fixing the designated prices, has 
conformed to those standards.”
The Supreme Court has since upheld many other grants of administrative 
authority in the face of plausible charges that their criteria for exercising 
power were no more specific than in the two found wanting in 1935. Even 
statutes of major pohtical and economic significance, containing provisions of 
great detail and complexity, often exhibit vagueness precisely at the point of 
critical policy choice. One can, therefore, see the Schechter and Panama 
Defining cases as “sports,” better explainable in terms of the politics of the 
justices of the Supreme Court in 1935 than in terms of legal doctrine. This 
explanation, however, does not give sufficient weight to other factors at work 
in those cases. Nor does it detract from the importance of the nondelegation 
doctrine.
